name: The Cities That Shaped the World
description: Rome to Singapore: how crossroads, harbours and planned capitals became centres of trade, power and ideas.

checkpoints.name: Cities of the ancient world
checkpoints.note: Athens became a school for the Mediterranean, and Rome rose from a river town to an empire. Alexandria, Chang'an and Samarkand sat on the roads where goods, scholars and religions met, and set the pattern of the capital city.

checkpoints.name: Capitals of faith and empire
checkpoints.note: London began as a Roman port, Constantinople as an emperor's new capital, and Baghdad as the seat of a caliphate. Kyoto was laid out by the Japanese court on a grid modelled on Chinese cities.

checkpoints.name: Medieval hubs
checkpoints.note: Cairo, Timbuktu and Venice grew rich on trade in grain, gold and spices, while Florence turned banking wealth into art. Across the Atlantic the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan rose from a lake island, and each city drew scholars, merchants and rivals from far away.

checkpoints.name: Ports and new capitals
checkpoints.note: European ships linked the continents. New cities such as New York, Saint Petersburg, Sydney and Singapore were built as ports or window-capitals, and Washington was laid out as a capital on paper first.

checkpoints.name: Cities on the drawing board
checkpoints.note: Canberra and Brasilia were designed from nothing as capitals, with competitions and famous architects. Their success and shortcomings are still argued by planners.

checkpoints.name: The age of megacities
checkpoints.note: Tokyo, Shanghai, Mexico City and Lagos grow from regional centres into cities of tens of millions as farmers move to town, and the largest cities now shift toward Asia and Africa.
